seoDesc: 20/20 Vision for 2020: work out risk of impairment (Smoking) from the activity. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator returns risk of impairment (Smoking) from the 23 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. That makes it useful for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator work?
sections.html:
The 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports risk of impairment (Smoking) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex, the household activities and the cycling, hiking, walking); then you type in the activity, the diet, for how many years? and the pack years.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Risk of impairment=(diet, activity, pack years)
Olive oil=-alcohol − cereals − dairy + diet − fish − red and white meat − vegetables, fruits and legumes
How many cigarettes?=20 × pack years ÷ for how many years?
Risk of impairment=(diet, activity, do you smoke?)
How active are you at work?=activity − (cycling, hiking, walking, household activities, gym, team sports)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Sex set to Male, How active are you at work? set to Moderately active, Household activities set to Less than two hours/week and Cycling, hiking, walking set to Less than two hours/week. Straight away the calculator returns Diet = 36.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Diet = 36 should be roughly the size you expected from Sex set to Male and How active are you at work? set to Moderately active.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the activity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns risk of impairment (Smoking), derived from the activity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the activity, which is 23 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (13 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Diet = 36. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the 20/20 Vision for 2020 calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
